steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a visualization paper presenting Chart2Vec, a model that learns a universal, context-aware embedding of visualizations. Motivate the need for it, explain the main challenges and how we address them, and finish with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Visualizations as data; why represent them generally
- Prior work: representation learning / embeddings for visualizations
- Gaps: task-specific, single-view only, no context
- Our aim and the three challenges (input embedding, dataset, learning tasks)
- Chart2Vec and its evaluation
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Visualizations as data
  - visualizations help people identify complex patterns, communicate insights
  - automatic methods speed up creation: improve dataset quality (cite), extract insights (cite), pick visual representation (cite)
  - users grasp key info more quickly, accurately, comprehensively (cite)
  - so many visualizations from experts + automated systems -> visualizations are a new format of data (cite)
  - worth studying general representation for downstream tasks: comparison, recommendation, assessment, querying (cite each)

  - inspired by representation learning; semantic vectors, i.e. embeddings (cite)
  - ChartSeer (cite): encoder-decoder, to/from embeddings, exploratory visual analysis
  - Li et al. (cite): structure-aware, better visualization retrieval, visual + structural info
  - vs heuristic/rule-based: more flexible, general; learned embeddings reusable for many downstream tasks
- Gaps
  - only one or two specific tasks (visual comparison, recommendation)
  - mostly single-view
  - multi-view: context info critical, affects later tasks
  - no universal representation that takes context into account
- Our aim + challenges
  - universal embedding of context-aware visualizations from associations in large corpus of visualization specifications
  - context-aware = co-occurrence and logical relationships in multi-view visualizations (narrative sequences in data stories, logical orders of visual analytic findings)
  - challenge 1: input embedding with semantic content + structural info
    - reviewed natural language descriptions of visualization data (cite); summarized key structural features from specifications
    - existing methods: only explicit info (chart types, data statistics, "data facts" (cite)); ours also implicit: field names, values, data semantics
  - challenge 2: large-scale context-aware dataset for training/test
    - multiple visualizations in a cohesive representation = multi-view visualizations (cite); dashboards, infographics, data stories
    - lack of good multi-view datasets with context
    - 849 data stories from Calliope (cite), 249 dashboards from Tableau Public (cite); 6014 visualizations total
    - public at https://chart2vec.idvxlab.com/
    - ten topics: economy, sports, society, health, politics, industry, recreation, food, education, ecology
  - challenge 3: deep learning tasks to learn context
    - supervised + unsupervised; linearly interpolated loss for sequentially connected charts (logical associations); triplet loss for co-occurrence
    - multi-task training; hyperparameters + automatic updates
- Chart2Vec + evaluation
  - learns universal embedding, extracts context-aware info, enables recommendations, storytelling, generation
  - ablation studies, user study, quantitative comparison with existing visualization embedding methods (cite)
- Contributions
  - dataset + input embedding (factual + semantic info)
  - Chart2Vec model
  - lessons learned

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Data visualizations are an important way to help people find complex patterns in data quickly and to communicate insights. There are automatic methods that make creating visualizations faster, by improving the quality of the dataset used for the visualization, by extracting the most meaningful information or insights from the data, and by choosing the right visual representation. This lets users get the key information from visualizations more quickly, accurately, and comprehensively. Because there are now so many visualizations made by experts and by automated systems, visualizations themselves have become a new format of data. So it is worth studying how to represent this visualization data effectively and precisely in a generalizable format, to support downstream visualization and visual analytics tasks like comparison, recommendation, assessment, and querying.

Representation learning has made a lot of progress recently, and several studies in the visualization community have tried to use semantic vectors (i.e., embeddings) to represent information from visualization data. ChartSeer for example used an encoder-decoder approach that converts visualizations to embeddings and back to help exploratory visual analysis. More recently Li et al. proposed a structure-aware method that improves visualization retrieval by considering both visual and structural information together. Representation learning gives a more flexible and general presentation of visualizations than heuristic or rule-based methods do. When the embedding features are learned, they can be used for many different downstream visualization tasks.

But these attempts can only be used for one or two specific visualization tasks, such as visual comparison and visualization recommendation. Also, most existing work focuses on tasks for single-view visualizations. For multi-view visualizations, the context information is a critical part of the representation and it influences the outcome of later tasks. There is still no universal representation of visualizations that takes context into account and can be used for different downstream tasks.

- Our aim + challenges
  - universal embedding of context-aware visualizations from associations in large corpus of visualization specifications
  - context-aware = co-occurrence and logical relationships in multi-view visualizations (narrative sequences in data stories, logical orders of visual analytic findings)
  - challenge 1: input embedding with semantic content + structural info; reviewed natural language descriptions of visualization data; explicit info (chart types, data statistics, "data facts") plus implicit info (field names, values, data semantics)
  - challenge 2: dataset; multi-view visualizations = dashboards, infographics, data stories; 849 data stories from Calliope, 249 dashboards from Tableau Public, 6014 visualizations; public at https://chart2vec.idvxlab.com/; ten topics: economy, sports, society, health, politics, industry, recreation, food, education, ecology
  - challenge 3: learning tasks; supervised + unsupervised; linearly interpolated loss (logical associations), triplet loss (co-occurrence); multi-task training, hyperparameters + automatic updates
- Chart2Vec + evaluation
  - universal embedding, context-aware info, recommendations/storytelling/generation
  - ablation studies, user study, quantitative comparison with existing embedding methods
- Contributions
  - dataset + input embedding (factual + semantic)
  - Chart2Vec model
  - lessons learned

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Data visualizations are an important way to help people find complex patterns in data quickly and to communicate insights. There are automatic methods that make creating visualizations faster, by improving the quality of the dataset used for the visualization, by extracting the most meaningful information or insights from the data, and by choosing the right visual representation. This lets users get the key information from visualizations more quickly, accurately, and comprehensively. Because there are now so many visualizations made by experts and by automated systems, visualizations themselves have become a new format of data. So it is worth studying how to represent this visualization data effectively and precisely in a generalizable format, to support downstream visualization and visual analytics tasks like comparison, recommendation, assessment, and querying.

Representation learning has made a lot of progress recently, and several studies in the visualization community have tried to use semantic vectors (i.e., embeddings) to represent information from visualization data. ChartSeer for example used an encoder-decoder approach that converts visualizations to embeddings and back to help exploratory visual analysis. More recently Li et al. proposed a structure-aware method that improves visualization retrieval by considering both visual and structural information together. Representation learning gives a more flexible and general presentation of visualizations than heuristic or rule-based methods do. When the embedding features are learned, they can be used for many different downstream visualization tasks.

But these attempts can only be used for one or two specific visualization tasks, such as visual comparison and visualization recommendation. Also, most existing work focuses on tasks for single-view visualizations. For multi-view visualizations, the context information is a critical part of the representation and it influences the outcome of later tasks. There is still no universal representation of visualizations that takes context into account and can be used for different downstream tasks.

We want to fill this gap, so we aim to propose a universal embedding of context-aware visualizations, based on associations derived from a large corpus of visualization specifications. Here context-aware means the co-occurrence and logical relationships within multi-view visualizations, for example narrative sequences in data stories and logical orders of visual analytic findings. There are several challenges. The first one is that we need a proper input embedding that uses both the semantic content and the structural information of each visualization. For this we reviewed related studies on natural language descriptions of visualization data and summarized the key structural features we can get from visualization specifications. Existing methods only extract explicit information like chart types and data statistics (sometimes called "data facts"), but our input chart embedding also considers implicit information, including field-related details from the dataset like field names, the corresponding values, and data semantics. The second challenge is that we need a large-scale dataset of context-aware visualizations for training and testing. Multiple visualizations in a cohesive representation can be seen as multi-view visualizations, and these give a comprehensive and contextual understanding of the data, in the form of dashboards, infographics, and data stories. There are no high-quality multi-view datasets with contextual information, so we collected and selected 849 data stories from Calliope, which is an online data story generation platform, and 249 dashboards from Tableau Public, which is an online platform for making and sharing data visualizations. In total there are 6014 visualizations. The dataset is publicly available at https://chart2vec.idvxlab.com/. It covers ten common topics: economy, sports, society, health, politics, industry, recreation, food, education, and ecology. The third challenge is that we need to set up several deep learning tasks to learn the contextual information from a set of input embeddings. We combined supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. We use a linearly interpolated loss function for charts that are connected sequentially to learn logical associations, and we use the triplet loss to capture co-occurrence of charts. We also use a multi-task training strategy and optimize the results with hyperparameter settings and automatic updates.

In this paper we propose Chart2Vec, which is a model that learns a universal embedding of visualizations, extracts context-aware information, and enables other downstream applications like recommendations, storytelling, and generation. To see how effective the model is, we did extensive evaluations, including ablation studies, a user study, and quantitative comparisons with existing visualization embedding methods.

To summarize, the main contributions of this paper are:

- We collect a high-quality context-aware visualization dataset and formulate an input embedding that includes both factual and semantic information.

- We present Chart2Vec, a representation model that learns a universal embedding of visualizations, extracts context-aware information, and enables various downstream applications.

- We summarize the key lessons we learned while designing and developing Chart2Vec, which we hope will help later visualization applications and related research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Data visualizations are an important means to help people quickly identify complex data patterns and communicate insights. Automatic methods help speed up the visualization creation process by improving the quality of the dataset used for visualization [1], extracting the most meaningful information or insights from the data [2,3], and selecting the appropriate visual representation [4,5]. This allows users to grasp the key information from visualizations more quickly, accurately, and comprehensively [6]. With so many visualizations created by experts and automated systems, visualizations themselves have become a new format of data [7]. It is therefore worth studying how to effectively and precisely represent such visualization data in a generalizable format to support downstream visualization and visual analytics tasks such as comparison [8], recommendation [9], assessment [10], and querying [11].

Inspired by recent advances in representation learning, several studies in the visualization community have tried to use semantic vectors (i.e., embeddings [12]) to represent information from visualization data. For example, ChartSeer [13] adopted an encoder-decoder approach that converts visualizations to and from embeddings to assist exploratory visual analysis. More recently, Li et al. [14] proposed a structure-aware method that improves visualization retrieval performance by considering both visual and structural information together. Compared to heuristic or rule-based methods, representation learning allows a more flexible and general presentation of visualization. Once the embedding features are learned, they can be applied to a variety of downstream visualization tasks.

However, these attempts to present visualizations through embeddings can only be applied to one or two specific visualization tasks, such as visual comparison and visualization recommendation. Moreover, most existing work focuses on single-view visualization tasks. For multi-view visualizations, context information is a critical aspect of visualization representation that influences the outcome of subsequent tasks. A universal representation of visualizations that can be used for various downstream tasks while taking contextual information into account is still lacking.

To fill this research gap, we aim to propose a universal embedding of context-aware visualizations based on the associations derived from a large corpus of visualization specifications. In this paper, context-aware refers to the co-occurrence and logical relationships within multi-view visualizations, such as narrative sequences in data stories and logical orders of visual analytic findings. Several challenges remain. First, we need to formulate a proper input embedding that uses both the semantic content and the structural information of each visualization. To do this, we reviewed related studies on natural language descriptions of visualization data [15,16] and summarized the key structural features that can be obtained from visualization specifications. Whereas existing methods only extract explicit information, such as chart types and data statistics (sometimes called "data facts" [17]), our input chart embedding also considers implicit information, including field-related details from the dataset such as field names, corresponding values, and data semantics. Second, a large-scale dataset of context-aware visualizations is needed to form the training and test datasets. Multiple visualizations in a cohesive representation can be regarded as multi-view visualizations [18], which provide a comprehensive and contextual understanding of the data in the form of dashboards, infographics, and data stories. Because high-quality multi-view datasets with contextual information are lacking, we carefully collected and selected 849 data stories and 249 dashboards from Calliope [2], an online data story generation platform, and Tableau Public [19], an online platform for creating and sharing data visualizations, respectively, for a total of 6014 visualizations. The dataset is publicly available at https://chart2vec.idvxlab.com/ and covers ten common topics, including economy, sports, society, health, politics, industry, recreation, food, education, and ecology. Third, we need to set up multiple deep learning tasks to learn the contextual information from a set of input embeddings. We integrated supervised and unsupervised learning tasks, using the linearly interpolated loss function for sequentially connected charts to learn logical associations and the triplet loss to capture the co-occurrence of charts. We also employ a multi-task training strategy and optimize the results by setting hyperparameters and automatic updates.

In this paper, we propose Chart2Vec, a model that learns a universal embedding of visualizations, extracts context-aware information, and enables other downstream applications such as recommendations, storytelling, and generation. To investigate the model's effectiveness, we conducted extensive evaluations, including ablation studies, a user study, and quantitative comparisons with existing visualization embedding methods [13,20].

In summary, the major contributions of this paper are as follows:

- • We collect a high-quality context-aware visualization dataset and formulate an input embedding that incorporates both factual and semantic information.

- • We present Chart2Vec, a representation model that learns a universal embedding of visualizations, extracts context-aware information, and enables various downstream applications.

- • We summarize the key lessons learned while designing and developing Chart2Vec, which we hope will benefit subsequent visualization applications and related research.
